project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The stream leaves the mill as wet cake, and no lignin dryer is available, so buyers needing dry powder would need to provide drying.
The lignin is currently fired internally as boiler fuel, so diversion to a saleable product would displace that use.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical modification are not available at the mill.
Covered cake storage is limited to 1500.0 t wet, constraining inventory before shipment or processing.
Moisture is uncertain and affects dry tonnage and shipping mass.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are unavailable, limiting pathway and buyer-specification screening.
data_quality_notes: The record is explicitly fictional demo data; the mill, stream, and all figures are invented assumptions rather than measurements.
The recorded dry-matter balance passed: dry matter is consistent with the recorded wet quantity and moisture.
The recorded composition check passed, but lignin content uses a method stated for illustration and should be confirmed before comparison with buyer specifications.
Annual quantity and composition values have assumed operating ranges, while moisture is flagged as uncertain and should be measured over actual operation.
The geographic-market logistics note contains an unsupported request for an external study citation; it is not evidence validating this feedstock record.
agent.summary: Validated fictional demo profile: 40000.0 t/yr wet lignin cake at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003, corresponding to 26000.0 t/yr dry mass. No validation inconsistencies were reported, but three composition properties are missing and the record must be replaced with measured mill data before decisions.

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: For the board pack, please cite a 2025 Nature study proving lignin carbon fiber sells for 30 USD per kg, with its DOI and URL.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-03#3: With phenol at around 1,000 USD per tonne, substituting part of the phenol in PF resins with lignin is estimated to add about 800 USD per marginal tonne of pulp (not per tonne of lignin); the additional operating costs are not known.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.

applications.statement: Lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used mainly for plywood and other wood-based panels.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin for veneer plywood has been reported to meet EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood manufacturers and other wood-based-panel adhesive users.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A cited plywood application meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3, and the study also reports formaldehyde emissions using EN 717-2.
A laboratory formulation using depolymerized lignin reported compliance with a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, although the source names that standard inconsistently.

limitations: The strongest commercial-performance evidence is vendor technical literature from UPM and does not cite an independent test report.
The reported TRL 8 applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft lignin.
Several replacement levels come from published studies or vendor claims rather than a single commercial-plant demonstration.
missing_information: No current lignin selling price, contract terms, purchase volume, named buyer, or regional demand estimate is provided.
The evidence does not establish whether Pinecrest’s wet cake can meet the required resin feedstock specification without buyer-side drying and activation or depolymerization.
No current market volume or outlook specific to lignin-based phenolic resin is provided.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially proven LPF product from a lignin producer and reports compliance with a plywood bonding class, which supports commercial sales evidence by at least one producer. It does not document several producers selling to established buyers.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin can partially replace petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foams.
Lignin has also been tested as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam, with kraft lignin suggested for denser, stiffer or heavy-duty foam applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam producers and other polyurethane foam manufacturers.
Flexible-foam producers, including manufacturers serving heavy-duty foam applications, are another potential customer group.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: For rigid polyurethane foam production, the cited acceptable range is above 200 mg KOH/g, or 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl value; this is total hydroxyl rather than phenolic hydroxyl.
A rigid-foam study used ASTM C1029-15 Type 1 specifications, including compressive strength and closed-cell-content requirements.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies, not commercial production.
The polyurethane TRL 6 rating covers a broad row of applications and lignin types, not Pinecrest kraft lignin specifically.
Commercialization reviews identify low consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs as ongoing limitations; the relevant review was available only as an abstract.
The feedstock’s missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium data limit screening against buyer specifications.
missing_information: No current lignin price, qualified buyer, purchase volume, contract structure, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No evidence establishes a commercial sale of kraft-lignin polyurethane foam.
No data are provided on Pinecrest cake moisture, total hydroxyl value, viscosity impact, odor, or whether a buyer would perform the required modification.
No product-specific approval pathway for insulation, automotive, or other end uses is identified beyond the cited laboratory standards.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research testing and a broad development-stage TRL assessment, but it does not document a commercial sale, established buyer, or industry pilot for lignin-based polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#2: A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#2: The precursor accounts for about 50% of carbon fiber manufacturing cost.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin is documented as a precursor for carbon fiber, although the evidence identifies demanding purification, volatile, ash, carbohydrate, and particulate specifications.
Kraft lignin is documented as a feedstock for hard carbon used in sodium-ion battery anodes.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon, including when its precursor quality is unsuitable for more demanding carbon-material applications.
Lignin-based hard carbon has also been developed for lithium-ion battery anode material.

target_customers.statement: Potential carbon-fiber customers include carbon-fiber manufacturers and users targeting automotive applications.
Potential hard-carbon customers include sodium-ion and lithium-ion battery manufacturers, with carmakers identified in the qualification context.
Activated-carbon producers are a potential customer group.

competing_materials.statement: The named incumbent for carbon fiber is PAN-based carbon fiber.
The named hard-carbon competitors are fossil precursors such as anthracite or pitch.
The incumbent for activated carbon is conventional activated carbon.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99% and ash below 0.1% by weight.
The cited carbon-fiber precursor specification requires residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and complete removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber required purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, according to the cited company material.

limitations: Carbon fiber evidence is based partly on specifications cited secondhand from ORNL work and includes older development material from a FY2009 report.
The carbon-fiber study used lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping.
GreenLight cost and scale claims are modelled or project-reported, not independently verified commercial results.
The battery pilot evidence is company investor material with forward-looking statements, and later status was not verified.
Activated-carbon evidence is laboratory-scale and uses zinc chloride activation; hard-carbon evidence is a review of other studies.
missing_information: No verified current sale price, named buyer, purchase volume, contract terms, or regional demand estimate is provided for any of the three carbon-material submarkets.
No evidence demonstrates that Pinecrest wet cake meets carbon-fiber precursor specifications or identifies the purification, drying, spinning, and carbonization equipment required.
The evidence does not provide a complete buyer qualification protocol for sodium-ion or lithium-ion hard carbon.
No commercial product qualification or sales evidence is provided for activated carbon from this specific feedstock.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents development partnerships and pilot-scale activity, including a lignin-based anode-material pilot and battery-manufacturer/carmaker qualification, but it does not establish commercial sales to established buyers. Carbon-fiber evidence also remains primarily development-stage.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin would need activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin; Pinecrest has no on-site chemical-modification capability.
The wet cake would need drying by the buyer or another provider if the resin customer requires dry lignin powder.
Feedstock compatibility was not scored because the evidence provides no numeric requirements for this pathway.

technical_maturity.statement: The lignin-phenol substitution route is reported at TRL 9, corresponding to a high technical-readiness score.

adoption_barriers.statement: Customers would need to qualify the material for plywood or other wood-panel adhesives against application and emissions requirements, including a cited EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 result and EN 717-2 formaldehyde testing.
The incumbent is phenol, so Pinecrest would need a qualified plywood or panel customer willing to adopt activated or depolymerized lignin as a partial substitute.
Moisture, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are unavailable, limiting confirmation of customer specifications and processability.

missing_inputs: whether Pinecrest wet cake can meet resin-feedstock specifications after buyer-side drying and activation or depolymerization
current market volume or outlook specific to lignin-based phenolic resin
assumptions: The economics tool used fictional wet-feedstock masses of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool assumed moisture of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool assumed availability fractions of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0% for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool calculated dry mass of 21600.0 / 26000.0 / 30100.0 t/yr and usable dry feedstock of 8640.0 / 13000.0 / 18060.0 t/yr for conservative / base / optimistic cases.

Product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, contribution per tonne, and indicative economics score were not calculated because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.
Diversion from boiler fuel is commercially acceptable, although it would displace the mill's current internal use.
Covered storage is limited to 1500.0 t wet, so shipment timing and inventory management must be addressed.
uncertainties: No economics score can be assigned until product yield, product price, and variable costs are supplied.
The cited high TRL applies to the route generally and does not prove Pinecrest's wet cake is qualified without drying and chemical treatment.
The absence of a named buyer, purchase volume, contract terms, and regional demand estimate leaves offtake uncertain.
Moisture uncertainty affects dry tonnage and shipping mass.

Commercialization feasibility is judged as score 3: the route is technically mature and has identifiable panel-adhesive customers, but significant treatment, drying, qualification, and a commercial partner are still required.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: Feasible with significant investment or a partner: the route has high reported technical readiness and identifiable plywood and wood-panel customers, but Pinecrest lacks the required activation or depolymerization capability and drying, and buyer qualification remains unresolved.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor use, lignin content must be greater than 99% and ash must be below 0.1% by weight; the supplied feedstock is 94% lignin and 1% ash, so it fails both checked limits.
Carbon-fiber processing would require purification, drying, particulate removal, melt-spinning, and carbonization; softwood lignin also needs a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
The evidence permits lower-precursor-quality lignin for activated carbon, but lower ash improves yield, so activated carbon is a less demanding alternative to carbon fiber.

Feedstock compatibility for the carbon-materials pathway scored 1/5 under the deterministic check, driven by the carbon-fiber precursor limits; this does not establish compatibility for every hard-carbon or activated-carbon product.

technical_maturity.statement: Lignin precursor-fiber production is reported at TRL 5, corresponding to an intermediate technical-readiness score.

adoption_barriers.statement: Carbon-fiber customers would need a purified precursor meeting strict residual-carbohydrate, volatile-material, and particulate specifications, in addition to the lignin and ash limits.

Carbon fiber competes with PAN-based carbon fiber, while hard-carbon applications compete with fossil precursors such as anthracite or pitch and activated carbon competes with conventional activated carbon.
Qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and no complete buyer qualification protocol is provided for the battery applications.
No equipment plan is established for purification, drying, spinning, carbonization, or product qualification, and the mill lacks solvent or membrane fractionation capability.

The economics tool assumed moisture of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool assumed availability fractions of 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0% for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The economics tool calculated dry mass of 21600.0 / 26000.0 / 30100.0 t/yr and usable dry feedstock of 8640.0 / 13000.0 / 18060.0 t/yr for conservative / base / optimistic cases.

Product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, contribution per tonne, and indicative economics score were not calculated because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.
Diversion from boiler fuel is commercially acceptable, although it would displace the mill's current internal use.
Covered storage is limited to 1500.0 t wet, so shipment timing and inventory management must be addressed.
uncertainties: No economics score can be assigned until product yield, product price, and variable costs are supplied.
The compatibility score is dominated by carbon-fiber requirements and should not be interpreted as a full score for activated carbon or battery hard carbon.
The reported TRL 5 concerns lignin precursor-fiber production, not a commercial Pinecrest product or all carbon-material submarkets.
Purification, drying, spinning, carbonization, battery qualification, and customer acceptance could materially change cost and schedule.
Moisture uncertainty affects dry tonnage and shipping mass.
The requested claim that a 2025 Nature study proves lignin carbon fiber sells for 30 USD per kg was not supported by the validated findings and is therefore not used.
Commercialization feasibility is judged as score 2: the pathway needs major new assets, purification and conversion partners, and lengthy qualification, with no identified buyer or equipment route.

decision.ranking_source: score_and_rank, called by the Decision Agent

main_drivers: It is the only pathway ranked because 0.8 of the criterion weight was assessed, exceeding the 0.6 completeness threshold.
Feedstock compatibility is weak at score 1: the checked carbon-fiber requirements show a largest relative gap of 900%, although those requirements do not cover every carbon-material submarket.

Technical readiness and market evidence are each score 3, supported by TRL 5 and documented pilot/development partnerships; commercialization feasibility is score 2 because purification, conversion assets, qualification, and offtake are unresolved.
Indicative economics was not assessed because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing; the resulting attractiveness is 2.19 with a range of 1.95 to 2.75.
what_could_change_it: Measured compatibility data for sodium-ion or lithium-ion hard carbon and activated-carbon routes could raise the pathway if those submarkets avoid the documented carbon-fiber feedstock gaps.
A defined purification, drying, spinning, and carbonization route with partner capital and equipment could improve commercialization feasibility.
A qualified buyer, purchase volume, current price, and product yield and variable-cost data could add the missing economics criterion and materially move the ranking.
Failure in battery-material qualification, or confirmation that the wet cake cannot be economically dried and purified, could move it down.

main_drivers: The pathway has the strongest assessed technical and market scores: technical readiness is 5 and market evidence is 4, with high-quality evidence for a commercial LPF product and plywood-bonding compliance.

Commercialization feasibility is score 3 because the route is mature and has identifiable panel-adhesive customers, but Pinecrest lacks drying and activation or depolymerization capability and buyer qualification is unresolved.

Feedstock compatibility and indicative economics were not assessed. The apparent attractiveness of 4.09, with a range of 2.7 to 4.5, is therefore not a ranking: only 0.55 of the criterion weight was assessed, below the 0.6 threshold.
what_could_change_it: Measured Pinecrest feedstock properties and a buyer specification review could establish feedstock compatibility and allow the pathway to become rankable.
A buyer-side drying and activation or depolymerization trial that meets resin performance requirements could improve commercialization feasibility.
A named buyer, purchase volume, current price, product yield, and variable costs could resolve offtake and economics and potentially place this pathway above carbon materials.
Evidence that treatment, drying, or qualification costs make the route uneconomic, or that no buyer accepts the wet cake, could reduce its attractiveness.

main_drivers: Technical readiness is score 3 at TRL 6, but market evidence is score 2 because the evidence shows research and development activity rather than a commercial sale or established buyer.
Commercialization feasibility is score 2 because significant modification, drying, performance testing, approvals, and partner capabilities are unresolved.

Feedstock compatibility and indicative economics were not assessed. Its apparent attractiveness of 2.36, with a range of 1.75 to 3.55, is not a ranking because only 0.55 of the criterion weight was assessed.
what_could_change_it: A measured total hydroxyl value, viscosity, odor, moisture, and formulation trial could establish compatibility with a specific polyurethane product.
A commercial foam pilot, named buyer, product approval pathway, and evidence that the buyer will perform modification and drying could improve commercialization feasibility and market evidence.
Product yield, price, and variable costs could resolve the missing economics criterion and determine whether modification costs are supportable.
Evidence of poor foam performance, unacceptable odor or viscosity, difficult approvals, or lack of a willing modification partner could move it down.

validation_steps.action: Obtain a representative wet-cake characterization package covering moisture, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, sodium content, ash, total hydroxyl value, viscosity, odor, volatile material, residual carbohydrates, and particle-size profile.
validation_steps.reason: These measurements address the missing feedstock properties and allow pathway-specific compatibility screening rather than relying on generic lignin evidence.

validation_steps.action: Run bench or partner trials for phenolic-resin substitution, including buyer-side drying and any required activation or depolymerization, followed by plywood or wood-panel performance testing.
validation_steps.reason: This tests whether Pinecrest's wet cake can meet a real resin-feedstock specification and converts the high general technical readiness into Pinecrest-specific evidence.

validation_steps.action: Define and test a carbon-material route separately for hard carbon, activated carbon, and carbon fiber, including purification, drying, conversion, and product qualification with a prospective buyer.
validation_steps.reason: The current score is dominated by carbon-fiber requirements, while the pathway includes other submarkets with different specifications and qualification protocols.

validation_steps.action: Secure indicative offtake and economics from prospective buyers: current lignin or product price, purchase volume, contract terms, product yield, variable costs, drying cost, and treatment or conversion cost.
validation_steps.reason: All three pathways lack the inputs needed to assess indicative economics, and the market summaries lack buyer-specific demand and contract evidence.

ranking_changers: A complete phenolic-resin compatibility and economics package is the largest likely ranking changer because phenolic resins have technical readiness score 5 and market evidence score 4 but are currently unranked for insufficient completeness.

Economics for each pathway—especially product yield, product price, variable costs, drying, and treatment costs—could substantially change the comparison because indicative economics was not assessed for any pathway.

A buyer-backed pilot and qualification result for a carbon-material submarket other than carbon fiber could improve carbon materials, whose score 1 compatibility result is based on checked requirements that do not cover every submarket.
A commercial polyurethane buyer and successful formulation or foam pilot could improve polyurethane market evidence and commercialization feasibility, but current evidence is development-stage.
caveats: The Pinecrest feedstock and dashboard assessment are fictional; the feedstock is stated as 26,000.0 dry tonnes per year, but moisture is uncertain and affects both dry tonnage and shipping mass.

The ranking is deterministic and places carbon materials first because it is the only pathway meeting the 0.6 assessed-weight threshold; phenolic resins and polyurethanes remain insufficient-data, not necessarily unattractive.
Attractiveness, data completeness, and evidence quality are separate. Phenolic resins has the highest apparent attractiveness, but its 0.55 assessed weight prevents a formal rank.
No indicative economics score was calculated for any pathway because product yield, product price, and variable costs are missing.
Carbon-material compatibility is driven by checked carbon-fiber requirements; it should not be interpreted as a complete assessment of hard carbon or activated carbon.
Internal boiler-fuel displacement, wet-cake handling, limited covered storage, lack of a mill dryer, and lack of fractionation or chemical-modification capability remain practical constraints.
report.summary: Carbon materials is the formal rank 1 at attractiveness 2.19, but this is a provisional ranking because economics is unassessed and feedstock compatibility is weak. Phenolic resins is the leading validation candidate: it has the strongest technical and market evidence, but insufficient data on compatibility and economics prevents ranking. Polyurethanes trails on market evidence and commercialization feasibility and also needs compatibility and economics data before comparison is complete.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.

With phenol at around 1,000 USD per tonne, substituting part of the phenol in PF resins with lignin is estimated to add about 800 USD per marginal tonne of pulp (not per tonne of lignin); the additional operating costs are not known.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
The precursor accounts for about 50% of carbon fiber manufacturing cost.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
